Formula recall · Part 4 · 29:00–32:00

Percent and average: name the whole

Percent memory sheet

Write the general percent-change rule and label its denominator.
Write multipliers for a rise, a fall, and two successive changes.

Data memory sheet

Write mean, total from a mean, and a combined-group mean.
Describe how to locate the median of an even-sized ordered list.
Two useful labels
“Change compared with what?” guards the percent base. “Total of what, shared among how many?” guards the average.
Formula recall · Part 5 · 32:00–35:00

Probability: say the event first

Retrieve the familiar rules

Write a probability ratio for equally likely outcomes, the complement relationship, and the no-replacement update.

Retrieve the counting test

Write a one-sentence test for arrangements versus selections. Use the words “swap” and “same outcome.”
Now scan your formula page. Circle only the gaps; rewrite those without looking.
Explain rather than recite
When can you multiply along a two-draw path? What changes after the first token is not put back?
Grammar recall · Part 1 · 35:00–38:00

Commas: boundaries, not breaths

Write four comma rules

Retrieve the rule for an introductory element, a series, a nonessential interruption, and joined independent clauses.

Test the boundaries

Add punctuation only where needed:

“After the bell rang the team packed notebooks pencils and maps.”

“The lights dimmed and the audience waited.”
Ask what the mark separates
Can both sides of the conjunction stand alone? Is the middle detail removable? Is this a real boundary or just a pause?
Grammar recall · Part 2 · 38:00–41:00

Does the clause identify or add?

Which / that / who / whom

Write the usual edited-English pattern for a restrictive versus nonrestrictive clause. Then describe how you test subject versus object within a clause.

Retrieve, then test

There are several lockers; identify one:
“The locker ___ has a dent is mine.”

There is only one library; add a detail:
“Our library ___ opens early is quiet.”

“The student ___ called left a note.”
“The student ___ we called left a note.”
Do not let the word choose for you
Removing the clause may leave grammar intact but change which person or thing is meant. Test identification first.
Grammar recall · Part 3 · 41:00–44:00

Find the controller of the word

Agreement

Level 1

“The box of markers (is / are) on the desk.”

Pronoun reference

Level 2

“When Leila handed Noor the folder, she smiled.”

Tense

Level 2

“Yesterday we measured the wall and record its length.”

Three small questions
What is the subject, not the nearby noun? Exactly who or what does the pronoun name? When does each action happen?
Grammar recall · Part 4 · 44:00–47:00

Choose the relationship before the word

Retrieve the logic families

Supply one transition for each relationship: addition, contrast, cause/result, example, and sequence.

Tiny on-screen rehearsal

Level 2

“The class labeled every tray. ___, two trays were still misplaced.”

“The path was flooded. ___, the group used another route.”

Read the completed sentence
If the relationship were wrong, could a sophisticated-sounding word make it right?
Grammar recall · Part 5 · 47:00–50:00

Support. Conclude. Belong.

Best supports

Level 2

Claim: “Clear labels reduce sorting mistakes.”

Best concludes

Level 3

A paragraph explains why a seed library makes seeds easier to share.

Relevance

Level 3

In that seed-library paragraph, a sentence lists the librarian’s favorite novels.

The final grammar check
Write one question you will ask before accepting a support sentence, a conclusion, or a sentence that is only loosely related.
Fiction locked block · Read · 50:00–53:00

The Doorway

1Mara arrived at the school auditorium with a floor plan folded into perfect squares. For the exhibition, she had placed every table so that visitors would follow a single smooth loop. When Eli rolled a cart of clay models toward the doorway, she checked his wheels against the arrows on her paper.

2Then the custodian tested the east door. Its lower edge scraped the floor and stopped. “This entrance stays closed until it is repaired,” he said. Mara stared at the beginning of her carefully drawn route. She set the plan on a table and pressed its curled corners flat, as though the paper might supply another door.

3“We can move the welcome table,” Eli offered. “People could come in from the courtyard.” Mara began to explain why the route had to start beside the photographs. Before she finished, two younger students arrived carrying a display too wide for the courtyard steps. Eli tilted his empty cart toward them. “Try this way.”

4Mara watched him guide the cart around the corner. Her arrows had accounted for tables, but not for someone arriving with both hands full. She took a pencil from behind her ear and drew a small cross through the welcome table. “Let’s leave room here,” she said. This time, she looked toward the doorway before drawing the next line.
